headline: NASA Readies Moon Base with Underground Shelters and Ice Hunt
meta_description: NASA launches three missions to find lunar caves, detect hazards, and locate water ice for humanity's first permanent Moon base.
summary_short: NASA is preparing humanity's first Moon base by searching for underground lava tubes that could shelter astronauts, tracking dangerous surface conditions, and hunting fo…
body:
NASA is moving closer to establishing humanity's first permanent Moon base through three new scientific investigations selected to unlock the secrets of long-term lunar survival. The missions will search for underground caves that could serve as natural shelters, investigate hidden deposits of water ice, and monitor environmental hazards threatening future explorers. These instruments and technologies, chosen through NASA's PRISM program, will be delivered to the lunar surface via the agency's Commercial Lunar Payload Services initiative—laying critical groundwork for the Artemis program and eventual human journeys to Mars.

The most striking possibility involves enormous lava tubes beneath the Moon's surface. One mission, called GIMLI, will examine the Marius Hills Pit, an opening that may connect to vast underground passages. These natural tunnels, formed when ancient lava cooled on the surface while molten rock flowed beneath, could provide astronauts with stable temperatures and protection from intense radiation and micrometeorite impacts—advantages no surface structure alone could offer. Dr. Nathaniel Putzig of the Planetary Science Institute will lead this investigation, using geophysical measurements to determine what lies below and whether these spaces are large enough to shelter humans.

A second mission, LEMS-SP, will establish an autonomous monitoring station at the Moon's South Pole to track moonquakes, micrometeorite strikes, and volatile substances in the lunar atmosphere. Meanwhile, the DISCO payload will make the first direct measurements of water ice hiding in micro-cold traps—exceptionally frigid regions shielded from sunlight. Confirming the presence and accessibility of this ice could transform lunar survival from theoretical exercise into practical reality, providing both drinking water and fuel for future missions. Together, these investigations represent science going first to the Moon, preparing not just equipment but knowledge itself for the astronauts who will follow.
quick_facts: Three NASA missions selected to study Moon's South Pole region for base construction
GIMLI will explore Marius Hills Pit for potential underground lava tube shelters
LEMS-SP monitoring station will track moonquakes and micrometeorite impacts
DISCO payload seeks water ice in extremely cold lunar surface regions
Findings support NASA's Artemis program and long-term lunar exploration goals
